I was recently rummaging through a storage closet, when I discovered a box I didn't recognize. Inside, I found the barely-used Recon Instruments Jet "smart glasses" that I had impulsively preordered back in 2013.

My original interest in the glasses was not for their designed purpose , but instead for the potential of hacking them into a HUD for my motorcycle helmet . Recon advertised that they planned to release a SDK, and for the purposes of my project, a weather-resistant $500 display was far more palatable than the delicate-looking waitlisted $1,500 Google Glass.

By the time they actually shipped in 2015, the public had developed strong opinions about people wearing internet-connected cameras on their faces. Undeterred, I was still hopeful that they would work for my helmet project, or would at least provide some utility on my daily bicycle commute to San Francisco.

My initial test wearing the glasses while on my bike was quite disappointing. Evaluating the product at face value (ha!), the Jet's apps just didn't provide enough added value to justify wearing them. You can get more accurate data from a $25 cycle computer, music sounds better in earbuds, and if you're lost on a bike or you get a text message, it takes 30 seconds to stop and peek at your phone.

The uninspiring default apps were not the showstopper for me, though. Setting aside the difficulty of getting used to the obtrusive opaque display mount, the optics were... bad. There wasn't much adjustability, and it was nearly impossible to get the display both fully in focus and fully visible at the same time. (The Terminator would have hated this display!) The bright backlight and soft-focused edges made the screen look more like an old CRT than anything out of my sci-fi fantasies. The Jet's UX was thus almost necessarily awkward, legibility concerns on the tiny panel dictating using a large font that limited how much information could be presented per screen. This then meant many more screens, and a lot of navigating and paging around with a temperamental touchpad.

I packed the glasses back into their case after a single ride, with the intent to sell them when I got around to it. However, at that time I was a preoccupied parent of a 2-year-old, and had just started a new job.

So, I instead immediately forgot they existed.

Until 12 years later!

Recon Instruments was acquired by Intel in 2015, and shut down in 2017 .

I didn't intend to launch into a project. I was just planning to reacquaint myself with the glasses, mostly to decide whether it was worth trying to sell them for beer money, or whether they were basically e-waste to recycle. Naturally, after over a decade, the batteries were very dead. Not only did they not hold a charge, but the Jet wouldn't even boot, even when plugged into USB. Before writing them off as scrap, I decided to first try some battery surgery. The battery module is a removable pod on the opposite arm from the display (which does a good job balancing the weight).

Inside the pod is a small charge management board (with 3 spring-loaded contacts) that also acts as the connection to the glasses, powered by a 490mAh 3.7v LiPo battery (701547). I have lots of 3.7v LiPos kicking around, but unfortunately all the wrong size. As a "temporary" test, I desoldered the old battery from the charge management board, and soldered in a larger battery via pigtails.

Once it had continuity to a battery with some voltage, the Jet booted right up!

But now they were in a weird state, cracked open, with an ugly battery dangling off the side. Nobody's going to buy them for cycling in this condition...

It was October 16, 2026. This context is important. I didn't have any plans for the glasses. But this was the month when the Internet collectively discovered they could use AI to reverse-engineer everything .

So naturally, I pointed Claude Code at the Jet and said "heyyyy...."

I have decades of experience writing high-level code, but I've also worked on a lot of low-level systems. I've written kernel drivers from hardware specs, reverse engineered proprietary code using only strace , used logic analyzers, soldered connections for snooping diagnostic ports, and spent considerable time poring over tcpdump logs. I've written compilers and built embedded systems for robots. My point is not to brag, but just to disclose the sort of knowledge I was bringing to the project. Having worked "close to the bits" certainly enables me to prompt more effectively than a total novice, but the sheer velocity of an LLM doing the heavy lifting was simultaneously amazing and ego-crushing. My experience just wasn't all that critical.

Within the first day, the Jet was rooted, the critical hardware was mapped out, and a replacement menu system was up and running on Android. On day two I decided I wanted to swap Android for Linux. The drivers for the display, input, battery management, and WiFi were all quickly ported. Rendering the kernel log to the display for debugging.

A weekend or so later, here's Claude's executive summary of the hardware situation:

> A Recon Jet (TI OMAP4430, 1 GiB, 8 GB eMMC, 428x240 Kopin microdisplay, camera, two mics, speaker, IMU, WiFi/BT) boots mainline Linux 6.18 from its eMMC boot partition in under four seconds to a live display, with the rooted stock Android kept in the recovery slot as a fallback. Every piece of hardware the project needs works from mainline: display, touchpad, both buttons, camera, WiFi, Bluetooth (LE keyboard paired), speaker, microphones, IMU, barometer, proximity "glance" sensor, board temperature, charger and fuel gauge, power LED, watchdog, RTC.. GPS works through the stock TI daemon in a chroot.

> Not ported: FM (removed driver), the Apple MFi coprocessor, and the speaker's DSP tuning.

I can't imagine how long it would have taken me to get to the same point coding all this on my own. Months? Years?

Although I didn't enjoy using the Jet as an end-user product, the physical hardware is pretty impressive for 2013. The designers were operating under extremely challenging space and power constraints, yet they crammed tons of functionality into a tiny space, and claimed a four hour runtime. Even after trying to build a "low power" mode, my replacement software runs extremely thirsty compared to the default product. (I'm constantly pulling over 300mA, yielding a battery life closer to 1 hour. Good thing I don't need to market and sell my version to bicycle-racing weight weenies ! For hacker glasses, a USB tether to a powerbank to extend runtime feels like a completely reasonable solution.)

As far as my application software goes, it's kind of a hot mess. When I started, I didn't have any concrete plans beyond a proof-of-concept: "replace the stock software". Without a concrete product in mind when I started, every time I subsequently had a new idea, it strained the architecture of the current implementation.

Where things landed is a compromise.

A small static C daemon ( jetd ) owns the panel and inputs, and is controlled using a line protocol on a local socket; a NodeJS application ( jet-app ) on the device owns the user interface as a set of "app mode" plugins.

There is a bit of awkwardness in that jetd does some UI on its own. Notably, it owns the kernel log display, and the interactive shell terminal. If jet-app isn't running and connected, jetd switches to a "deadman" mode to enable access to these low-level tools.

Platform capabilities (provided via Linux kernel drivers and the jetd daemon):

- Local graphics API to draw to the display

- Microphone access

- Speaker access

- Input via two buttons plus a trackpad to detect swipes

- Shell mode

- Kernel log mode

- Networking via WiFi and USB

- mDNS publishing as jet.local

- VPN access via WireGuard (to access my homelab services)

- Remote ssh

- Bluetooth keyboard

- Camera image capture

- Glance detection

- GPS

- IMU

- Power management

- Remote API for debugging, system settings, camera capture, and remote "screen sharing", including audio and inputs.

The system was ready to build... something. But what?

Having abandoned the idea of using the Jet in my motorcycle helmet, I had a few alternative project ideas that intrigued me:

- Augmented senses. Could the glasses continuously provide extra information about the world that either I can't normally see, or that I'd need to do extra work to interpret? Examples: automatically show QR/bar code information, compute and compare unit pricing for products at the supermarket, interpret resistor color codes when I'm at my workbench, show nearby wifi networks, recognize and deep-dive specs for ordinary things around me, etc. It turned out that the Jet's camera's focus and exposure weren't well-suited for tasks like desk-distance resistor band identification, so I quickly realized this idea had some basic hardware limits attached. I still like the basic concept of augmented senses a lot, though. It's the primary feature I'd want from real AI glasses.

- An OSINT interface. Inspired by God's-Eye View , display relevant info about my location on a continuously updated map, such as crime alerts and known surveillance cameras; allow viewing real-time stream from public traffic cameras. While this seemed cool at first (in addition to too many sci-fi movies, I've watched too many spy movies) I then realized that not only do I not need a real-time intel feed to survive my bike ride to the coffee shop, my town is pretty boring, and any data would be limited and repetitive. (There was a fire a few blocks away... three weeks ago, and yep, the Flock camera is stillll on the corner!)

- In the late 90's, I had been fascinated by Thad Starner's work at MIT Media Lab on wearable computing, in particular the concept of a " remembrance agent " - a continuously running automated information retrieval system displaying a feed of relevant stored memories. I wondered if I could build a lightweight version of this idea. It seemed like it could pair well with an augmented senses feature.

As a general rule, when the scope of your "weekend project" starts bumping into someone's PhD thesis, it's probably time to reassess the feasibility of your plans!

AI glasses are not a solved problem, so it was clear further work on this project would require endless iteration. Alexa and Siri provided a sobering reminder that commercial AI products with huge development budgets and years of development remain frustratingly crude and limited... and I'd be tackling this with precisely zero experience building even a basic interactive voice assistant, never mind one with a camera and lots of other sensors!

Even armed with agentic superpowers, I had to concede that almost any useful AI glasses build would require far more work than reasonable for a one-off hack... especially for a one-off hack motivated more by engineering curiosity than any actual intent to actually... use them.

I thus decided that the milestone for "Part 1" of this project should be far more humble, focusing simply on exercising end-to-end functionality:

A decade ago, even this would have been a huge project. In 2026, it proved to be completely reasonable, providing valuable experience in building a different type of agentic loop than I had every built before. I even went a bit beyond the basics. To make things more interesting, I decided that instead of building a generic "helpful assistant", it would be more fun to give it some personality. I also built in a (very) rudimentary "world model" to capture details of things seen by the camera.
